How Do Screw-Retained Implant Teeth Stay Aligned?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

If you have been researching dental implants or have recently had treatment, you may have come across the term screw-retained implant teeth and wondered how they actually stay in place and remain aligned over time. It is a common and very reasonable question, particularly for patients who are comparing implant options or trying to understand what happens inside their mouth after treatment.

Screw-retained implant teeth are a widely used restoration method in modern implant dentistry. Unlike cement-retained crowns, they are secured directly to the implant fixture or abutment using a small titanium screw. This design aims to provide stability, retrievability, and precise alignment — but many patients are unsure how that alignment is actually maintained.

This article explains the mechanics behind screw-retained implant alignment, the clinical factors that contribute to long-term stability, and when it may be helpful to seek professional dental advice. Understanding this topic can help you make informed decisions and communicate more confidently during dental consultations.

What Are Screw-Retained Implant Teeth?

Before exploring alignment, it is worth briefly understanding what screw-retained restorations are and how they differ from other implant options.

A dental implant system generally consists of three components: the implant fixture (the titanium post placed into the jawbone), the abutment (a connector that sits above the gum line), and the crown or prosthetic tooth (the visible replacement tooth).

In a screw-retained system, the crown is attached directly to the implant or abutment using a small titanium screw that passes through the crown and locks into the implant body. This contrasts with cement-retained crowns, which are bonded onto an abutment using dental cement.

The screw-retained approach is often favoured by clinicians because it allows the restoration to be removed if necessary — for maintenance, adjustment, or repair — without damaging the crown or the surrounding tissue. The access hole through which the screw is inserted is typically sealed with a tooth-coloured composite material once the restoration is in place.

Screw-retained restorations are commonly used for single-tooth replacements, implant-supported bridges, and full-arch implant cases. Understanding how they are designed to stay aligned begins with understanding the role of implant placement.

The Role of Implant Placement in Long-Term Alignment

One of the most significant factors governing how well a screw-retained crown stays aligned is the position and angulation of the implant fixture itself at the time of surgical placement.

For a screw-retained crown to sit correctly in the mouth — aligning with adjacent teeth, matching the bite, and allowing the retaining screw to be accessed without creating aesthetic or functional problems — the implant must be placed at a very specific angle and depth within the jawbone.

Experienced implant clinicians use surgical guides and, increasingly, digital planning tools to map out the ideal implant position before surgery. Cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) scans allow a three-dimensional view of the jaw, identifying available bone volume, nerve positions, and the precise angle required for restoration alignment.

If an implant is placed at an angle that does not correspond to the planned restoration, achieving correct crown alignment becomes more challenging. This is why implant placement and restorative planning are closely coordinated — ideally by the same clinician or by a team working from the same digital plan.

Bone healing around the implant — a process called osseointegration — also plays a role. Once the implant integrates with the surrounding bone, it becomes a fixed anchor point. This stable foundation supports the aligned restoration over time.

The Mechanical Science Behind Screw-Retained Alignment

Understanding how screw-retained implant teeth stay aligned requires a look at the mechanical engineering principles involved.

The Implant–Abutment Interface

At the heart of the system is the connection between the implant fixture and the abutment. Modern implant systems use precisely engineered internal or external connection geometries — such as internal hex, conical, or morse taper connections — which physically interlock when assembled. These connection designs resist rotational and lateral forces, meaning the crown cannot easily twist or shift from its intended position.

The geometry of the connection is machined to very fine tolerances, often within microns. This precision is what allows the crown to be seated in exactly the same position every time it is placed, which is particularly important in multi-unit restorations where several components must align simultaneously.

Screw Torque and Clamping Force

The retaining screw plays a critical mechanical role. When tightened to the manufacturer's recommended torque — typically between 15 and 35 Newton-centimetres depending on the implant system — the screw generates a clamping force that holds the abutment and crown firmly against the implant.

This clamping force must be sufficient to resist the functional loads placed on the tooth during chewing and speaking, without being so great that it risks fracturing the screw or stripping the thread. Clinicians use calibrated torque wrenches to ensure the correct force is applied.

Occlusal Load Distribution

The crown is also designed so that biting forces are distributed in a way that does not destabilise the connection. When the bite is correctly calibrated — a process called occlusal adjustment — the forces during chewing are directed along the long axis of the implant, reducing lateral stress on the screw connection.

How Crown Fabrication Supports Alignment

The physical design of the crown itself is an important part of how screw-retained implant teeth stay aligned. Modern implant crowns are typically designed using computer-aided design and computer-aided manufacturing (CAD/CAM) technology.

Digital impressions or scanned models of the mouth are used to design a crown that accounts for:

  • The precise angulation of the implant
  • The position and height of adjacent natural teeth
  • The bite relationship (occlusion)
  • The aesthetic appearance in the context of surrounding dentition

The screw access channel — the small hole through which the retaining screw is tightened — must exit the crown in an accessible position, ideally on the palatal or occlusal surface (the inside surface facing the palate or the biting surface), so that it does not compromise aesthetics and can be accessed by a clinician if the crown ever needs to be removed.

In cases where implant angulation makes a straight-line screw access difficult, angled screw channel abutments can be used. These allow the screw to be angled slightly so the access hole exits in a more aesthetically or functionally appropriate position.

Laboratory-fabricated or digitally milled crowns are checked for fit on working models and sometimes directly in the mouth before final seating, ensuring the crown aligns correctly with adjacent teeth before the screw is tightened.

What Can Affect Screw-Retained Implant Alignment Over Time?

While screw-retained restorations are designed for long-term stability, certain clinical and patient-related factors can affect alignment over time.

Screw Loosening

One of the most commonly reported issues with screw-retained restorations is screw loosening. This can occur if the screw was not tightened to the correct torque, if there is a mismatch in the fit of the crown, or if the patient applies unusual forces — such as from clenching or grinding (bruxism).

A loose screw may cause the crown to feel wobbly, or patients may notice a slight change in their bite. This is generally a manageable issue: the clinician can remove the crown, check the components, and retighten or replace the screw as appropriate.

Bone Changes Around the Implant

Gradual changes in the jawbone around the implant — which can occur due to gum disease, systemic health changes, or mechanical overload — may affect the position of the implant over time. If the bone support around an implant changes significantly, the relationship between the crown and surrounding teeth may be affected.

Adjacent Tooth Movement

Natural teeth can shift position over time due to various factors, including tooth loss elsewhere in the mouth, age-related changes, or the absence of orthodontic retention. If adjacent or opposing teeth shift, the implant crown — which cannot move as it is fixed within bone — may appear out of alignment relative to the surrounding dentition.

Poor Initial Occlusal Balance

If the bite is not carefully balanced at the time of fitting, uneven force distribution can increase stress on the implant components, potentially contributing to screw loosening or, in rare cases, implant-level complications.

Preventing Misalignment: What Patients Can Do

Patients play an important role in supporting the long-term stability and alignment of screw-retained implant restorations. While clinical factors are largely managed by the dental team, certain everyday habits and routines make a meaningful difference.

Attend regular dental reviews. Routine follow-up appointments allow clinicians to check the torque on retaining screws, assess gum health around the implant, and identify any early changes in bite alignment before they become more complex issues.

Maintain excellent oral hygiene around the implant. Although implants cannot develop decay, the surrounding gum tissue and bone can be affected by bacterial buildup. Using interdental brushes, floss, or water flossers around the implant crown helps preserve the soft tissue and bone that support the restoration.

Inform your dentist if you clench or grind your teeth. Bruxism places significant off-axis forces on implant components and natural teeth alike. A clinician may recommend an occlusal splint (night guard) to protect the restoration during sleep.

Avoid using your implant crown to open packaging or bite hard objects. While implant crowns are designed to withstand normal biting forces, applying excessive or unusual force can increase the risk of component stress.

Report changes promptly. If you notice any movement, change in bite, unusual sounds when chewing, or discomfort around the implant, arrange a dental review rather than waiting for a scheduled appointment.

When Professional Dental Assessment May Be Appropriate

There are several situations in which it would be sensible to contact a dental professional regarding a screw-retained implant restoration:

  • You notice movement or wobble in the implant crown, which may indicate screw loosening
  • Your bite feels different, as though the crown is higher or lower than usual
  • You experience sensitivity or discomfort in the area around the implant, particularly when biting
  • The crown appears to have shifted visually relative to adjacent teeth
  • You see or feel the retaining screw access hole has opened (the composite seal has come loose)
  • There is any swelling, redness, or discharge around the gum tissue near the implant

None of these situations should cause undue alarm — many are straightforward to resolve clinically — but they do warrant timely professional attention rather than a wait-and-see approach.

Full-Arch Implant Restorations and Alignment Considerations

Alignment becomes an even more critical consideration in full-arch implant restorations — such as implant-supported bridges or full-arch fixed prostheses — where multiple implants must work together as a coordinated system.

In these cases, all implants must be placed with an awareness of how the final prosthesis will sit across the arch. Even small deviations in implant angulation can have a compounding effect when multiple units are connected.

Clinicians planning full-arch cases typically use virtual surgical planning software to simulate the entire case before any surgery takes place. This allows the team to evaluate how implant positions will interact with the planned prosthesis, adjusting the plan digitally before committing to surgery.

The prosthesis itself is designed with passive fit in mind — meaning it should seat onto all implant abutments simultaneously without requiring force. A prosthesis that does not fit passively can introduce stress at individual implant sites, potentially affecting long-term stability.

Our team in London works with a range of full-arch implant solutions. If you would like to understand more about what these involve, our full-arch dental implant treatment page provides a helpful starting point.

Key Points to Remember

  • Screw-retained implant teeth stay aligned through a combination of precise implant placement, engineered connection geometry, correctly torqued retaining screws, and accurately fabricated crowns.
  • The position of the implant at the time of placement is the single most important factor in determining how well the restoration will align with the surrounding teeth.
  • CAD/CAM crown design and digital planning tools help ensure crowns are fabricated to match the implant angulation and bite relationship before fitting.
  • Screw loosening is manageable and one of the more common minor issues — it can usually be resolved by a clinician tightening or replacing the retaining screw.
  • Regular dental reviews are important for checking component integrity, gum health, and bite alignment around implant restorations.
  • Patients with bruxism should discuss protective options, such as a night guard, with their clinician to reduce excessive force on implant components.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can screw-retained implant crowns become misaligned after fitting?

In most cases, a well-placed and correctly fitted screw-retained crown remains stable for many years. However, minor changes can occur — such as screw loosening, adjacent tooth movement, or gradual bone changes — which may subtly affect alignment. This is one of the reasons why regular dental reviews are recommended after implant treatment. If you notice any change in how your crown sits or feels, it is worth arranging an appointment rather than waiting for a routine check-up. Most alignment-related issues are straightforward to assess and manage clinically.

How does the dentist know if the implant crown is correctly aligned before fitting?

Before a screw-retained crown is finally seated, clinicians typically check the fit and alignment carefully. This may include using X-rays to confirm the seating of the crown on the abutment, assessing the bite with articulating paper to identify any high points, and visually comparing the crown with adjacent teeth. In some cases, a trial seating is carried out before the screw is permanently tightened and the access hole is sealed. Clinical assessment at this stage is important to ensure long-term comfort and stability.

What happens if the retaining screw becomes loose?

If the retaining screw loosens, patients may notice a slight movement of the crown, a change in bite, or a clicking sensation. This is not an emergency, but it does require prompt dental attention. The clinician will typically remove the crown, check all components for damage, clean and reassemble them, and retighten the screw to the correct torque. In some cases, a new screw may be fitted. Screw loosening does not necessarily mean the implant itself has failed.

Is screw-retained better than cement-retained for alignment?

Both approaches have their place in implant dentistry and each has clinical advantages depending on the situation. Screw-retained restorations are generally considered easier to retrieve and adjust, which can be beneficial if alignment or fit needs to be reassessed. Cement-retained restorations may be preferred in certain aesthetic zones where screw access positioning is challenging. The choice between the two depends on individual clinical factors, and your implant dentist will recommend the most appropriate option following assessment.

How long do screw-retained implant restorations typically last?

With appropriate care and regular professional maintenance, screw-retained implant restorations can last many years. The implant fixture itself — once fully integrated with the bone — is designed for long-term use. Individual components such as crowns or screws may require replacement over time due to wear or damage. Long-term outcomes are influenced by oral hygiene, general health, bite forces, and how consistently a patient attends for review appointments. A qualified clinician can give a more personalised perspective during a consultation.

Does grinding or clenching affect screw-retained implant alignment?

Bruxism — the habit of clenching or grinding the teeth, often during sleep — can place significantly elevated forces on implant restorations. Over time, this may increase the risk of screw loosening, component wear, or changes to the bite relationship. Patients who grind their teeth are often advised to wear an occlusal splint (night guard) to protect implant restorations and natural teeth alike. If you are aware that you grind your teeth, this is important information to share with your implant clinician before and after treatment.

Conclusion

Screw-retained implant teeth stay aligned through a carefully coordinated combination of surgical precision, mechanical engineering, and skilled restorative dentistry. From the initial positioning of the implant fixture in the jawbone to the tightening of the titanium retaining screw to the correct torque, every stage of the process contributes to the stability and alignment of the final restoration.

For patients, understanding the principles behind screw-retained alignment can help set realistic expectations and highlight the importance of ongoing maintenance. Regular dental reviews, good oral hygiene, and prompt attention to any changes in how the crown feels or looks are all meaningful contributions to long-term implant success.

If you have questions about your own implant restoration — whether you are in the planning stages, have recently completed treatment, or are experiencing any changes — a clinical assessment is always the most appropriate next step.
